The Bengal famine during the Second World War

The Bengal famine of 1943 was one of the most severe humanitarian disasters of late colonial India. It occurred during the Second World War, when military requirements and disruptions to trade placed considerable pressure on food supplies and distribution.

Its causes cannot be explained simply as a failure of monsoon rainfall. The disaster involved agricultural difficulties, wartime disruptions, rapidly rising food prices and failures of supply management.

Major causes of the 1943 famine

Reduced rice production

The important aman rice crop harvested towards the end of 1942 was poor. This reduced the rice supplies available for the following year.

Stocks carried over from earlier years were also inadequate to provide a substantial reserve.

Loss of rice imports from Burma

Burma had been an important source of rice for markets in the region. Following Japanese occupation during 1942, the established flow of rice imports from Burma was disrupted.

This placed additional pressure on Indian rice markets and contributed to Bengal's supply difficulties.

Wartime disturbances and rising prices

Wartime military demands and disruption of normal trade increased pressure on the distribution system. Rice prices rose sharply.

When prices increased, households dependent on low wages or irregular employment found it increasingly difficult to buy sufficient food.

Inadequate distribution and relief

Food did not reach all vulnerable households in adequate quantities or at affordable prices. Delays and weaknesses in government arrangements for moving supplies and providing relief aggravated the crisis.

The famine demonstrates the importance of both food supply and effective access to that supply.

The Bengal famine of 1943 involved wartime disruption, a poor rice harvest, loss of Burmese rice imports, high prices and inadequate distribution. It should not be explained as a famine caused by drought alone.

Consequences of the Bengal famine

Large numbers of people suffered severe hunger and malnutrition. Many left their villages in search of food, employment or assistance.

Malnutrition increased vulnerability to disease, and substantial mortality continued in the aftermath of the most acute food shortages.

The Government of India's Famine Inquiry Commission investigated the crisis and published its report in 1945. The report identified deficiencies in food supplies, problems in market distribution and serious weaknesses in the response to distress.

Historical estimates of famine mortality differ because contemporary registration was incomplete and deaths from subsequent disease must also be considered. The secure conclusion for basic prelims study is that the famine caused extensive mortality and displacement, with its effects extending beyond 1943.

Demographic consequences of colonial famines

Demographic impact means the effects of an event on a population, including its size, distribution, mortality and migration.

Repeated famines contributed to several important demographic and social consequences in colonial India.

1. Excess mortality

Severe famines caused deaths through starvation, malnutrition and disease. Mortality could remain high even after harvest conditions improved because weakened populations were vulnerable to infection.

2. Migration and displacement

People moved from affected villages towards towns, relief centres and other regions in search of food or employment. Some returned after conditions improved, while others settled elsewhere.

Migration therefore changed the distribution of population, even when the total population of a region was not permanently reduced by the same amount.

3. Loss of agricultural livelihoods

Farmers could lose livestock, seeds, tools or other productive resources. Agricultural labourers could lose employment when cultivation declined.

Such losses made recovery difficult and could leave families dependent on borrowing or migration after the immediate famine had ended.

4. Poverty and indebtedness

Households sometimes sold assets or borrowed money to purchase food. Debt could continue long after rainfall and agricultural production returned to normal.

5. Effects on population growth

Frequent famine mortality, inadequate nutrition and poor public health contributed to the difficult demographic conditions of colonial India.

NCERT identifies 1921 as an important dividing point in India's demographic transition. Before 1921, population growth remained low and irregular under conditions of high mortality. The second stage of demographic transition began after 1921, with death rates declining while birth rates remained high.

However, this overall demographic pattern was influenced by several factors, including diseases, health conditions and mortality, and should not be attributed exclusively to famines.

1921 is a demographic landmark, not a famine date. The year is important for understanding changes in India's population growth pattern during the colonial period.

How infrastructure and famine history are connected

Railways and telegraphs changed the ways in which goods, people and information moved across India.

Railways could transport grain and relief supplies, while telegraphs could communicate information about shortages, prices and the need for assistance.

However, neither system automatically guaranteed that poor households could obtain sufficient food. The effectiveness of relief depended on timely government action, available supplies, functioning transport and people's ability to access food.

The two parts of this subtopic therefore explain a common historical relationship: improvements in transport and communication can increase economic connections without automatically eliminating poverty or food insecurity.

One-glance revision of the complete subtopic

Three distinctions to remember

  • Railway versus telegraph: Railways transported goods and people; telegraphs transmitted information.
  • Drought versus famine: Drought refers to deficient rainfall; famine refers to a severe crisis of access to food.
  • Food supply versus purchasing power: Grain may be available in a market even when some households cannot afford to buy it.

Prelims focus

  • 1942: The poor aman rice harvest and disruption of Burmese rice imports preceded the Bengal famine.
  • 1943: Bengal famine during the Second World War.
  • 1945: Government of India's Famine Inquiry Commission report on Bengal.
  • Famine mortality includes deaths related to malnutrition and disease, not only direct starvation.
  • Migration, livestock losses and indebtedness were important social and demographic consequences.
  • 1921 is an important landmark in India's demographic transition.
  • Trap: More extensive railways and telegraphs did not automatically prevent famine or guarantee access to food.
